h1: Hop aroma descriptors on supplier sheets
title: Reading Hop Aroma Descriptors | Craft Beer School
desc: What the aroma words on hop supplier sheets really mean, where they come from, why the beer may not match them and how to build your own hop notes.
teaser: Every hop sheet promises tropical fruit and citrus. Here is how to read past the adjectives to the numbers that matter.
standfirst: Hop supplier sheets mix hard data with soft descriptors such as passion fruit, pine and stone fruit. Both are useful, but only if you know where they come from and what they cannot tell you.
sections: What a hop sheet usually contains

A typical supplier sheet lists the variety, origin and crop year, then analytical figures: alpha acids, beta acids, cohumulone as a share of alpha, total oil in millilitres per 100 grams and often a breakdown of the main oils. Underneath sit the aroma descriptors, a handful of words like citrus, tropical, grapefruit or herbal.

The numbers are measured on a sample of the lot or the crop. The descriptors are a summary of how the variety typically smells. They are not the same kind of information. They deserve different levels of trust.

Aroma descriptors usually start with breeders and growers describing a new variety, then get refined through trade panels and brewers' experience. Many are based on the smell of the raw hop, often from a rub test: a few pellets or cones rubbed between the palms and smelled.

That is valuable, but it describes the hop, not the beer. Some aromas survive the kettle and fermentation well. Others change, fade or appear only after yeast has worked on them. Descriptors can also be written with marketing in mind, especially for new proprietary varieties.
Why the beer may not match the sheet

Several things change the aroma between the sheet and the glass:

  • Crop year and region: the same variety grown in different places or seasons can smell different.
  • Harvest timing: earlier or later picking shifts the oil balance.
  • Processing and storage: warm storage loses the lighter, fresher oils first.
  • Biotransformation: yeast can convert some hop compounds, for example geraniol into citronellol, changing floral notes towards citrus.
  • The rest of the recipe: malt, yeast esters and water all shape how the hop reads.

A hop described as tropical can taste mostly piney in a heavy, malty beer. Treat descriptors as a hint about direction, not a promise.
Link the words to the oils

The oil breakdown on the sheet often explains the descriptors. Some broad links that most brewers use:

  • Myrcene: green, resinous, citrus. High in many American aroma hops.
  • Humulene: woody, herbal, the noble-type character of many European hops.
  • Caryophyllene: spicy, woody, peppery.
  • Linalool: floral, with orange and bergamot notes.
  • Geraniol: floral and rose-like.

Thiols, present at tiny concentrations, are behind blackcurrant, passion fruit and sometimes catty notes. They rarely appear on standard sheets. Our guide to catty notes in hoppy beer covers that side.

The one floor detail worth practising: read the total oil figure before the adjectives. A hop with very low total oil will not deliver a big aroma, whatever the words say.

The best check is your own nose. When a new lot arrives:

  1. Take a few pellets from a freshly opened bag.
  2. Rub them firmly between clean, unscented palms to warm and break them.
  3. Cup your hands and smell in short sniffs.
  4. Write down what you smell before you read the sheet.
  5. Compare with the previous lot of the same variety.

A lot that smells cheesy, musty or oddly weak has likely been stored badly. That is worth raising with the supplier before the hops go into a beer. Our guide to hop varieties for beginners covers the main families to compare against.

Over time, keep a simple record for each variety and lot: the sheet's descriptors, your rub notes, the oil figures and how the finished beer tasted. After a few lots, you will know which suppliers' words match your experience and which tend to oversell.

Use a shared vocabulary across your team so that citrus means the same to everyone. Reference aromas help: a fresh orange, a grapefruit, pine needles, a ripe mango. Our guide to choosing hops for hop water shows how clearly hop aroma reads when nothing else is in the way.

A good supplier will answer specific questions. Before you commit to a contract quantity of an aroma hop, ask for:

  • The certificate of analysis for the actual lot, not a typical sheet.
  • The crop year and growing region.
  • The packing date and how the hops have been stored since, including the temperature in transit to India.
  • The oil breakdown, if it is not on the sheet.
  • A sample you can rub test and, ideally, brew a small trial with.

Write the answers down next to your own rub notes. A supplier whose descriptors consistently match your nose is worth more than one with the most exciting adjectives. Over a few seasons, that record also tells you which varieties are worth fighting for and which are easily replaced.

Hop sheets are a starting point for choosing varieties, not a replacement for tasting. Connecting the chemistry on the sheet to what you smell and taste is a skill that improves with structured practice.

Your first step: take the hops currently in your store, do a rub test on each and write your own three descriptors before reading the supplier's words.
faqs: Where do hop aroma descriptors come from?
Mostly from breeders, growers and trade panels describing the raw hop, often from rub tests. They describe the hop, not necessarily the finished beer.
Why does my beer not taste like the hop description?
Crop year, storage, yeast biotransformation and the rest of the recipe all change hop aroma between the bag and the glass.
What is a hop rub test?
Rubbing a few pellets or cones between clean palms to warm and break them, then smelling. It is a quick way to check a hop lot's aroma.
